title: Infantile Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
description: Confirm with ultrasound rather than palpation, correct the metabolic alkalosis before anesthesia, and perform a pyloromyotomy, laparoscopically where the expertise exists.
objectives: Diagnose pyloric stenosis with ultrasound using a muscle thickness threshold
Resuscitate and correct metabolic derangement before surgery, knowing the apnea risk
Compare laparoscopic and open pyloromyotomy outcomes
Recognize postnatal erythromycin as a risk factor

references.citation: van den Bunder FA, Derikx JP, Kiblawi R, et al. Diagnostic accuracy of palpation and ultrasonography for diagnosing infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Radiol. 2022;95(1139):20211251.
van den Bunder FAIM, van Wijk L, van Woensel JBM, et al. Perioperative apnea in infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: A systematic review. Paediatr Anaesth. 2020;30(7):749-758.
Hall NJ, Pacilli M, Eaton S, et al. Recovery after open versus laparoscopic pyloromyotomy for pyloric stenosis: a double-blind multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2009;373(9661):390-398.

Oomen MW, Hoekstra LT, Bakx R, et al. Open versus laparoscopic pyloromyotomy for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis focusing on major complications. Surg Endosc. 2012;26(8):2104-2110.
Murchison L, De Coppi P, Eaton S. Post-natal erythromycin exposure and risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Pediatr Surg Int. 2016;32(12):1147-1152.

start.text: A 5-week-old boy has had 4 days of forceful, non-bilious vomiting after every feed, and he feeds hungrily again afterward. He was given erythromycin at 10 days old; postnatal erythromycin in the first 2 weeks is strongly associated with pyloric stenosis (OR 12.89 in a meta-analysis). He looks mildly dehydrated.

diagnose.text: No olive-shaped mass can be felt during a test feed. Next?

options.label: No palpable olive, so pyloric stenosis is excluded
options.feedback: In a meta-analysis of 43 studies (6,085 infants), the sensitivity of palpation ranged from 10% to 93.4% and has fallen over time. A negative examination does not exclude pyloric stenosis; ultrasound is the most accurate test.

options.label: Abdominal ultrasound, using a pyloric muscle thickness of 3 mm or more
options.feedback: Ultrasound has the highest diagnostic accuracy. A pyloric muscle thickness of 3 mm or more had pooled sensitivity of 97.6% and specificity of 98.8%, and the review authors advise that cut-off. Palpation sensitivity ranged from 10% to 93.4%.

prepare.text: Ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis. Bloods show a hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. The on-call team offers theatre tonight. What do you do?

options.label: Operate tonight before the electrolytes are corrected
options.feedback: Correcting metabolic derangements before surgery is the generally accepted practice, intended to prevent apnea. Infants with pyloric stenosis have high rates of perioperative apnea: 27% preoperatively and 0.2–16% postoperatively in a systematic review, although the link to alkalosis is unproven.

options.label: IV resuscitation and correction of the electrolytes and alkalosis first, then pyloromyotomy
options.feedback: It is generally assumed that metabolic derangements should be corrected before surgery to prevent apnea. A systematic review found apnea in 27% of infants before surgery and 0.2–16% after, though no study had tested the association with alkalosis.

approach.text: His electrolytes are corrected. Your unit performs laparoscopic pyloromyotomy routinely. Which approach?

options.label: Laparoscopic pyloromyotomy
options.feedback: In a double-blind RCT, laparoscopy shortened time to full feeds (18.5 vs 23.9 hours) and postoperative stay (33.6 vs 43.8 hours), with similar complications; the authors recommend it in centers with laparoscopic experience. In a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs (502 infants), laparoscopy did not significantly increase major complications (4.9% in the laparoscopic group).

options.label: Open pyloromyotomy, because laparoscopy has more major complications
options.feedback: In a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs, laparoscopic pyloromyotomy did not lead to significantly more major complications than open surgery, and full feeds came about 2 hours sooner. In the largest RCT, laparoscopy shortened time to full feeds and hospital stay with similar complications.

fail_missed.text: Diagnostic Error: Pyloric stenosis missed on examination alone.

fail_apnea.text: Safety Risk: Anesthesia before metabolic correction.

fail_slower.text: Slower Recovery: Open pyloromyotomy where laparoscopy was available.

success.text: Case Complete: Diagnosed by ultrasound, corrected, and repaired.
